question: What is the primary physiological goal of hemostasis in the body?

options.A: To speed up the overall circulation of red blood cells
options.B: To stop bleeding at injury sites while keeping blood fluid
options.C: To destroy foreign pathogens entering through broken blood vessels
options.D: To transport vital nutrients to damaged tissues during healing

explanation: Hemostasis stops bleeding at injury sites while maintaining normal fluid blood flow throughout the rest of the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: Secondary hemostasis differs from primary hemostasis because secondary hemostasis specifically involves...

options.A: immediate constriction of smooth muscle in the vessel wall
options.B: the physical removal of dead tissue surrounding the wound
options.C: the activation of plasma clotting factors to form fibrin
options.D: the rapid adhesion of circulating platelets to exposed collagen

explanation: Secondary hemostasis specifically utilizes plasma proteins called clotting factors to build a strong fibrin meshwork. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: What chemical substance acts as a vital bridge for platelet adhesion to exposed collagen?
explanation: Von Willebrand factor acts as the molecular bridge that helps platelets stick to exposed subendothelial collagen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient with a deficiency in thromboxane A2 release will most likely experience problems with...

options.A: producing adequate plasma clotting factors in the liver
options.B: recruiting and aggregating additional platelets to form a plug
options.C: initiating the initial vascular smooth muscle contraction spasm
options.D: dissolving the hardened fibrin clot after the tissue heals

explanation: Thromboxane A2 is released by activated platelets to recruit more circulating platelets for proper aggregation and plug formation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which specific substance triggers the extrinsic coagulation pathway upon tissue trauma?
explanation: Tissue factor is released into the blood following tissue trauma to rapidly trigger the extrinsic clotting pathway. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why is the intrinsic pathway given its name?

options.A: It bypasses all intermediate steps to activate fibrinogen instantly
options.B: All the necessary clotting factors are present directly within the circulating blood
options.C: It relies entirely on external tissue damage outside the blood vessel
options.D: It functions exclusively inside the specialized chambers of the human heart

explanation: The intrinsic pathway is so named because all components needed to initiate it are intrinsic to the circulating blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary enzymatic function of thrombin in the common pathway?

options.A: Stimulating immediate vascular smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Activating initial platelets by releasing von Willebrand factor
options.C: Breaking down the established fibrin mesh during repair
options.D: Converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin

explanation: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that form the structural foundation of the blood clot. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the specific function of Factor XIII within the clotting cascade?

options.A: Transforming inactive prothrombin directly into active thrombin
options.B: Cross-linking and stabilizing the formed fibrin threads
options.C: Attaching circulating platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen
options.D: Triggering the extrinsic pathway through tissue trauma release

explanation: Factor XIII acts as a cross-linking agent that stabilizes the loose fibrin mesh to make the clot firm and durable. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which active enzyme is primarily responsible for breaking down and dissolving a blood clot during fibrinolysis?
explanation: Plasmin is the active enzyme that digests fibrin strands to dissolve unneeded blood clots during fibrinolysis. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h5)

question: What physical change happens to the blood clot during the process of clot retraction?

options.A: It converts back into soluble fibrinogen proteins within the plasma
options.B: It expands outward to fill the entire lumen of the blood vessel
options.C: It instantly liquefies through the rapid release of local tissue factor
options.D: It shrinks in size and squeezes out serum to pull wound edges together

explanation: Platelet contraction during clot retraction pulls the clot tighter, expelling serum and drawing the vessel walls closer. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which circulating plasma protein works to neutralize excess thrombin and Factor Xa?
explanation: Antithrombin III is a major natural anticoagulant that binds to and inactivates thrombin and Factor Xa. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the protein C and protein S pathway?

options.A: Degrading active clotting factors like Factor V and Factor VIII
options.B: Stimulating vascular smooth muscle cells to undergo spasm
options.C: Converting inactive prothrombin into functional thrombin enzymes
options.D: Binding free floating platelets to damaged subendothelial collagen

explanation: Proteins C and S work together as a regulatory system to deactivate specific clotting factors and prevent excessive clotting. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which laboratory test is specifically used to monitor the effectiveness of heparin therapy?
explanation: The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) evaluates the intrinsic pathway and is used to monitor heparin therapy. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h7)

question: A patient taking warfarin for stroke prevention requires routine monitoring of which specific laboratory value?
explanation: The International Normalized Ratio (INR) standardizes prothrombin time to safely monitor patients taking oral anticoagulants like warfarin. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h7)

question: Hemophilia A is primarily caused by a genetic deficiency of which specific clotting factor?
explanation: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of clotting Factor VIII. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h8)

question: Why does disseminated intravascular coagulation paradoxically lead to severe bleeding despite widespread clotting?

options.A: Excessive amounts of circulating heparin neutralize all remaining plasma proteins
options.B: Vascular smooth muscle cells fail to undergo any initial constriction
options.C: The liver stops producing fibrinogen entirely due to sudden systemic inflammation
options.D: Micro-clots consume available platelets and clotting factors, leaving none for active wound sites

explanation: Widespread clotting in DIC depletes platelets and coagulation factors, causing severe hemorrhaging throughout the body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h8)
